rationale: The literature consistently supports the frequent co-occurrence of muscular hypotonia with congenital joint contractures, scoliosis, and distal arthrogryposis in individuals with biallelic FILIP1 variants. Furthermore, specific craniofacial features including facial hypotonia and high-arched palate are explicitly documented. However, the claim that hypotonia predominantly manifests as isolated craniofacial and axial hypotonia rather than generalized hypotonia is conflicted: foundational cohort descriptions (e.g., Schnabel et al., Roos et al.) document generalized muscular hypotonia, congenital myopathy with myofibrillar breakdown, and diffuse motor developmental delays across affected individuals.

evidence.text: Five affected individuals from three families with homozygous truncating FILIP1 variants presented with congenital contractures affecting shoulder, elbow, hand, hip, knee, and foot, alongside scoliosis, microcephaly, facial dysmorphism, and muscular hypotonia.

conflicts: While several case reports emphasize prominent facial hypotonia and axial deformities such as scoliosis alongside contractures, muscle biopsy and functional studies demonstrate underlying core-like congenital myopathy and general muscular weakness, contradicting the assertion that hypotonia is selectively craniofacial/axial rather than generalized.

new_directions.question_text: Does quantified neuromuscular testing differentiate proximal vs distal limb tone from axial/facial tone across all molecularly confirmed FILIP1 patients?
new_directions.rationale: Standardized motor scoring and muscle ultrasound/MRI can objectively measure whether hypotonia is primarily axial/craniofacial or part of a generalized myopathic tone reduction.

new_directions.question_text: Do missense variants preserving truncated FILIP1 domains cause a different tone profile than biallelic complete loss-of-function deletions?
new_directions.rationale: Differences between Roos et al. (missense and nonsense variants with congenital myopathy) and pure loss-of-function/deletion cohorts may explain variations between generalized flaccidity vs isolated contractures with facial weakness.
